cards.text: Job lost his children and his health (Job 1:18-19; 2:7), and three friends have been sitting with him (Job 2:11). One of them, Eliphaz the Temanite, just finished telling him that a wicked man writhes in pain all his days (Job 15:20). Now Job answers, and friend, this is NOT a thank-you card.

cards.question: Job says he's heard plenty of speeches like the one Eliphaz just gave. What does he call his friends?

cards.text: Then Job asks, "Is there no end to your long-winded speeches?" Friend, I've watched a cold oven preheat faster than these guys wrap up.

cards.question: Job says that if his friends were in his place, he could heap up words against them and shake his head at them.
But Job says that's not what he'd actually do. If his friends were in his place, what would Job use his mouth for?

cards.text: Then Job says talking doesn't relieve his pain, and holding back won't make it go away. It's like a smoke alarm after a burnt batch: wave a towel at it, it beeps; leave it alone, it BEEPS.

cards.question: Job says God has worn him out. What does Job say God has devastated?

cards.text: Job says his own frailty rises up and testifies against him. Then he says, "His anger has torn me and opposed me; He gnashes His teeth at me."
And Job isn't done. He says, "They open their mouths against me and strike my cheeks with contempt; they join together against me."

cards.question: Job says God has delivered him to unjust men and thrown him to the clutches of the wicked.

cards.text: Job says, "I was at ease, but He shattered me." Friend, I went from the kitchen counter to the back of a junk drawer in one day, and that was a paper cut next to THIS.

cards.question: Job says God's archers surround him, and God has set Job up as His ___.

cards.text: Job says He pierces him without mercy and breaks him with wound upon wound. Then Job says, "He rushes me like a mighty warrior."
Job has sewn sackcloth over his skin and buried his horn in the dust. His face is red with weeping, and deep shadows ring his eyes.

cards.question: Yet through all of it, Job says his hands are free of ___ and his prayer is ___.
Job asks the earth to cover his blood and let his cry for help be laid to rest.
Job doesn't want his cry for help silenced. And he says that even now, his witness is somewhere. Where?

cards.text: Then Job says, "My friends are my scoffers as my eyes pour out tears to God." Ouch, friend. Just ouch.

cards.question: Job wishes a man could plead with God the way he pleads with his ___.
Job gives a reason for that wish. When only a few years are past, what does he say will happen to him?

answers.text: He will go the way of no return
He will move to a far country
He will stand before the king

cards.text: Job keeps going, and it doesn't get any lighter. He says, "My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; the grave awaits me."

cards.question: Job already called his friends his scoffers. Now who does he say surrounds him?

cards.text: Then Job says, "Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand. Who else will be my guarantor?" Basically, who's going to co-sign for me, and friend, I don't see anybody around him reaching for a pen.

cards.question: Job says the ones whose minds have been closed to understanding will be exalted.

cards.text: Job says if a man denounces his friends for a price, the eyes of his children will fail. Then he says, "He has made me a byword among the people."

cards.question: Job says he's become a byword among the people, a man in whose ___ they spit.

cards.text: Job says his eyes have grown dim with grief, and his whole body is but a shadow.

cards.question: Job says the upright see what's going on here. How do they react?
Yet Job says a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows ___.

cards.text: Then Job turns to his friends and says, "But come back and try again, all of you." Sounds like an open invitation, right? Hang on.

cards.question: Job tells his friends he expects to find a wise man among them.

cards.text: Job says his days have passed and his plans are broken off, even the desires of his heart. Then he says, "They have turned night into day, making light seem near in the face of darkness."
Then Job pictures it. What if he looks for Sheol as his home, spreads out his bed in darkness, and calls corruption his father and the worm his mother or his sister?

cards.question: If Sheol is where Job ends up, what question does he ask?
Job asks whether his hope will go down with him to the gates of Sheol, into the dust.

cards.text: And that's where Job leaves it, with a question hanging in the dust. Keep your apron on, friend, because Job's story is far from over.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 11 quotes "I was at ease, but He shattered me.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 5 quotes "He has made me a byword among the people.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Several story cards are plain verse paraphrase with none of Papa Dorin's voice: stop 1 cards 8, 13 and 14, and stop 2 cards 5, 7 and 12. Stop 2 card 5 also gives no context for the line about denouncing friends for a price, so the moment doesn't make sense to the baker.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess the exact word in an unseen line. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason from meaning to 'neighbor' over 'brother' or 'king', so it's a wording guess.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The question opens with 'Job already called his friends his scoffers,' which is a near-synonym of the right answer 'Mockers.' That hands the baker the answer and rules out 'Soldiers' and 'Lions.'

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The question rewords Job 17:13's condition 'If I look for Sheol as my home' as 'If Sheol is where Job ends up.' That changes what the text says. Job is picturing looking for Sheol as his home, not simply ending up there.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.
